artworks.title: The Combat of Diomedes
artworks.description: Albertina drawing by the young David: Athena-fired Diomedes rampages across the Trojan plain — Iliad 5's aristeia as neoclassical frenzy, the mortal who wounds Aphrodite and Ares.

artworks.title: Diomedes and Glaucus Exchanging Armour
artworks.description: Gela pelike: after the day's slaughter, Diomedes and Glaucus refuse to fight and trade armour — gold for bronze, Iliad 6's pause that closes the aristeia with guest-friendship.

artworks.title: Diomedes (Roman copy after Kresilas)
artworks.artist: Unknown (Roman copy after a Greek original attributed to Kresilas)
artworks.description: Louvre Ma 890: the athletic Argive type — taut, alert, the warrior of the great day when Athena made him match even the gods in battle.

films.title: Helen of Troy
films.description: Wise's epic keeps Diomedes among the Greek captains at Troy — the Argive who, in Homer, dares to wound gods and still rarely gets the close-up.

popCulture.title: Iliad
popCulture.description: Books 5–6: Athena fires Diomedes to wound Aphrodite and Ares, then he and Glaucus trade gold armour for bronze between the lines — Homer's great day of Argive glory.

popCulture.title: Diomedes
popCulture.description: The son of Tydeus who alone among Homer's mortals wounds two Olympians in one day — the aristeia that defines his star.

popCulture.title: Glaucus of Lycia
popCulture.description: Guest-friendship mid-battle: Diomedes and Glaucus refuse to fight and exchange armour — gold for bronze, the Iliad's most famous pause in slaughter.
